sections.title: Mental model — the hi-lo guessing game

blocks.md: **Ask a yes/no question whose answer throws away HALF the suspects. Repeat until one suspect remains.**
Dictionary hunt: open middle page — too far? whole right half dies. Too early? left half dies. You never read pages linearly; you BISECT. Binary search is that instinct, coded.

steps: Too small → everything LEFT of mid dies (lo = mid+1)
Too big → right half dies (hi = mid−1)

items.q: Why can we discard a whole half?
options: sorted order proves target lives on one side only
items.explain: Order gives certainty — no checking needed on dead side.

items.q: Doubling items 1000→2000 adds how many checks?
items.explain: Halving chain grows by one link. That's why it scales.

blocks.label: iterative binary search
blocks.py:
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] == target: return mid
    if a[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1   # discard left incl mid
    else:               hi = mid - 1   # discard right incl mid
return -1                              # space empty -> absent

blocks.title: Trace: search 6 (absent) in same array — watch space die

blocks.md: **Two exits, both honest:** equal → position found; empty range → proven absent. Never loop forever: mid±1 always shrinks range.

blocks.label: recursive twin (same logic)

options: mid already tested & rejected — keep it and you may loop forever
items.explain: Infinite-loop insurance: progress guaranteed each round.

items.q: 8 items need at most how many checks?

blocks.md: Duplicates? Finding ANY match is easy; finding FIRST or LAST needs discipline: on match, don't stop — RECORD it and keep hunting that direction.

blocks.label: first occurrence

blocks.md: **Count occurrences** = last − first + 1. Two hunts replace full scans. This exact shape returns as lower_bound/upper_bound at L2.

items.title: Classic Binary Search
items.statement: Implement iterative version; then recursive twin.

solutionCode.label: iterative, then the recursive twin

items.complexity: Time O(log n) — the range halves each step. Space O(1) iterative, O(log n) stack recursive.

followups.q: Why `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` rather than `(lo + hi) / 2`?
followups.a: With lo and hi both near INT_MAX their sum overflows and goes negative, producing an out-of-bounds index. The subtraction form never exceeds hi. It is the single most famous bug in binary search — it sat in the JDK for nine years.

followups.q: Why `lo <= hi` and not `lo < hi`?
followups.a: With `<`, the loop exits while one candidate is still unexamined, so a target sitting at that final position is missed. `<=` keeps going until the range is genuinely empty. Test a single-element array: `lo < hi` never enters the loop at all.

items.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower
items.statement: API guess() says hi/lo/equal — pure guessing game.

solutionCode.label: same skeleton, comparison delegated to the API

items.complexity: O(log n) calls to the API. Space O(1).

followups.q: What is the trap in the API's sign convention?
followups.a: It is inverted from what feels natural: `guess(mid) == 1` means *your guess was too low*, so the answer is higher and lo must move up. Reading it as "the answer is 1 = higher than mid" happens to give the same action, but reading it as "mid is greater" flips the branches and fails every test. Read the contract, do not infer it.

followups.q: Why is the range 1..n rather than 0..n-1?
followups.a: The problem picks a number in [1, n], not an array index. Binary search does not require an array at all — it needs an ordered domain and a comparison. That is the bridge to searching over answer values later in this module.

items.title: First & Last Occurrence Pair
items.statement: Both boundaries in O(log n); output {-1,-1} if absent.
hints: Two hunts: mirror the while-condition branch.
lastOcc: on match go RIGHT instead.

solutionCode.label: two boundary hunts: on a match, keep going the other way

items.complexity: Two O(log n) hunts. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why record the match instead of returning immediately?
followups.a: Plain binary search returns the first index it happens to land on, which for duplicates is an arbitrary one in the run. Recording it and continuing to search the side where an even earlier (or later) copy could live is what pins down the true boundary.

followups.q: What is the only difference between the two hunts?
followups.a: One character of direction: on a match, the first-occurrence hunt moves `hi` left, the last-occurrence hunt moves `lo` right. Everything else is identical — which is why they collapse into one lambda with a flag rather than two copy-pasted functions.

items.title: Count Occurrences of x
items.statement: Use B103 results: count = last − first + 1.

solutionCode.label: count = last - first + 1

items.complexity: O(log n) — reuses the two boundary hunts. Space O(1).

followups.q: What happens without the absent check?
followups.a: Both hunts return −1, so the arithmetic gives −1 − (−1) + 1 = 1 — reporting one occurrence of a value that is not there. The guard is not defensive tidying; it is the difference between right and wrong.

followups.q: Why is this O(log n) rather than O(n)?
followups.a: Counting duplicates by scanning outward from a found index is O(k) for k copies, which is O(n) when the whole array is one value. Two boundary hunts stay logarithmic no matter how long the run is.

items.title: Sqrt(x) — integer floor
items.statement: Floor square root WITHOUT library. Search space 1..x/2+1.
hints: Predicate: mid*mid ≤ x — remember last such mid.

solutionCode.label: search the value space; remember the last feasible mid

followups.q: Why is hi = x/2 + 1 a safe upper bound?
followups.a: For x ≥ 2 the square root never exceeds x/2 — since (x/2)² = x²/4 ≥ x whenever x ≥ 4, and x = 2, 3 are covered by the +1. Starting at hi = x would also work but wastes a couple of iterations. Justifying the bound beats guessing it.

followups.q: Where is the overflow?
followups.a: mid can approach x/2, so mid*mid approaches x²/4. With x near INT_MAX that is far past 32 bits and wraps negative, making the comparison pass when it should fail. Casting one operand to long long before multiplying fixes it — casting the result afterwards is too late.

items.title: Search Insert Position
items.statement: Index where target belongs if inserted — first element ≥ target.
hints: Absent → answer lands at lo when loop ends.

solutionCode.label: hunt the first element >= target

followups.q: Why initialise ans to a.size() rather than -1?
followups.a: If every element is smaller than the target, it belongs after the last one — index n. Seeding with n makes that case fall out with no special handling. Seeding with −1 would return a nonsense index for the largest targets.

followups.q: What is this function actually called?
followups.a: lower_bound. "Insert position" and "first element ≥ target" are the same question, which is why the same code answers B106, B107 and half of B202. Recognising that identity is worth more than memorising three variants.

items.title: Ceil of x in Sorted Array
hints: Same shape as B106 without insert semantics.
Track candidate whenever a[mid] ≥ x, go left.

solutionCode.label: same lower-bound hunt, returning the value

followups.q: How would you get the floor instead?
followups.a: Mirror every direction: accept when a[mid] <= x, record it, and move lo right to look for a larger candidate. The two functions are reflections of each other — one shape, two directions, which is the whole lesson of this pair.

followups.q: Why is −1 a risky sentinel here?
followups.a: It collides with real data — an array containing −1 makes "not found" indistinguishable from "the ceiling is −1". Returning an index (or n) is safer, or an optional. Worth flagging even when the constraints promise positive values, because constraints change.

items.title: Nearly Sorted Array Search
items.statement: Element may sit at i−1, i, or i+1 of its sorted home. Modified BS.
hints: Check mid, mid−1, mid+1 before discarding.
Discard TWO elements per round — still logarithmic feel.

solutionCode.label: check mid-1, mid, mid+1 before discarding either side

items.complexity: O(log n) — the range still shrinks by roughly half each step, just by 3 indices at a time instead of 1. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why jump by 2 rather than 1?
followups.a: You just examined mid−1, mid and mid+1 and ruled all three out. Moving lo to mid+1 would re-test a known-miss. Jumping to mid+2 discards three indices per round instead of one — still logarithmic, with a slightly better constant.

followups.q: Why must the neighbour checks be bounds-guarded?
followups.a: mid−1 can fall below lo and mid+1 above hi, especially in the last couple of iterations. Without the guards you read outside the active range — in C++ potentially outside the array — and can return an index that was already excluded.

items.title: Binary Search Recursive Trace Practice
items.statement: Hand-trace recursive bs() for {2,4,6,8,10}, target 8 — write call stack like Foundations L2.

solutionCode.label: recursive search that records its own call stack

items.complexity: O(log n) time, O(log n) stack. Depth for n = 5 is about log₂5 ≈ 3 frames.

followups.q: Trace {2,4,6,8,10} for target 8.
followups.a: Frame 1: lo=0, hi=4, mid=2, a[2]=6 < 8 so go right. Frame 2: lo=3, hi=4, mid=3, a[3]=8 — hit, return 3. Two frames, not three: the range shrank from 5 candidates to 2 to a hit. log₂5 ≈ 2.3 is the ceiling, and landing early is normal.

followups.q: When does recursion depth actually matter?
followups.a: At log₂(10^9) ≈ 30 frames it never will — binary search cannot blow a stack. Depth matters for recursion over n frames, like naive linked-list recursion. Knowing which recursions are shallow by construction is what stops you converting them to loops for no reason.

items.title: Odd Occurring Element (XOR bridge preview)
items.statement: Every element twice except ONE, pairs adjacent, array sorted-by-pairs. Binary-search the break point.
hints: If a[mid]==a[mid^1] pattern intact on left → break right.
XOR trick: mid^1 gives its partner index.

solutionCode.label: pair parity: XOR the index to find its partner

followups.q: What does mid^1 compute?
followups.a: It flips the lowest bit, so even index i maps to i+1 and odd index i maps to i−1 — exactly the partner slot under the pairing 0-1, 2-3, 4-5. It saves branching on whether mid is even or odd, which is the version most people write first.

followups.q: Why `lo < hi` here when B101 used `lo <= hi`?
followups.a: This is a converging search, not a match search: it narrows to a single surviving index rather than testing for equality. `hi = mid` (not mid−1) keeps mid as a live candidate, so `lo <= hi` would never terminate. Match-style and converge-style searches have different termination conditions — mixing them is the classic infinite loop.

n items ⇒ ~log₂n checks; doubling input adds ONE check
Pairs-array odd-element: partner index mid^1 detects break side
